messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. Eduardo Reyes, a 67-year-old physician of Latin American descent, had spent decades calmly managing medical emergencies, but nothing had prepared him for the moment his own son, Mateo, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive leukemia when the boy was twelve. Eduardo still could not assemble the events of those first weeks into a clear story—fragments of white hospital walls, the hematologist’s voice going hollow, Mateo’s small hand gripping his own during the first lumbar puncture. He knew the facts, but when he tried to recall the sequence, the narrative fell apart, leaving him with only a blurred sense of dread and a strange inability to find words for what had happened. This incomplete picture itself became intolerable; to avoid the dizziness of reaching for a memory that would not come, Eduardo began to actively push the whole experience out of his mind. If a thought about the illness emerged, he would immediately switch on the television or pull up a medical journal on his tablet, keeping his mind occupied at all times. He told himself it was the only way to stay functional.

But the threat kept breaking through. Even years later, long after Mateo had gone into remission, Eduardo could not sit in a waiting room without his pulse racing, scanning every parent’s face for signs of panic. The sound of a child crying in a nearby examination room would trigger a flashback so vivid that he felt his own nostrils fill with the antiseptic smell of the oncology ward, and he would have to grip the edge of his desk to keep from acting as if his son were still lying in that bed. These surges of hypervigilance and raw guilt only intensified his determination to block out the past. The more he felt the flashbacks coming, the more aggressively he distracted himself—reviewing lab results on his phone during lunch, volunteering for extra shifts so that his evenings held no silence. Unwittingly, this very suppression made the memory even less coherent. By refusing to think about the trauma, Eduardo never allowed his mind to piece together a full narrative, and the gaps in his recollection grew wider, leaving him more vulnerable to sudden, fragmentary intrusions.

The cycle tightened over the months and then years. He noticed that his own mental strategies—the constant mental chatter, the refusal to let his mind wander—began to wear him out. He became startlingly vigilant behind the wheel, checking his rearview mirror obsessively as if an ambulance might appear, even though his son was now a healthy young man. He recognized, with a physician’s clinical detachment, that his attempts to avoid thinking about the trauma were actually making him more alert to threat cues, not less. But knowing this did not stop him. By his late sixties, Eduardo lived alone in a quiet suburban house, deliberately single and socially withdrawn, because the emotional exposure of dating or even casual friendship seemed too risky; any question about his family could pull him toward the memory he had fought so hard to suppress. He had transformed his professional environment—a large community hospital—into a controlled space, arranging his clinic hours to minimize overlap with pediatric patients and always entering the building through a back corridor to avoid the waiting room where parents sat with pale children.

What finally brought Eduardo to seek help was a moment of collapse. During a routine staff meeting, a colleague mentioned a new leukemia protocol, and Eduardo felt his throat close. He excused himself, but instead of recovering, he stood in the restroom unable to recall why he had even gone into the room. The gaps in his own mind now frightened him more than the original trauma. He made an appointment with a psychologist, terrified that if he tried to tell the story of Mateo’s illness aloud, he would lose the words and never get them back. He came not expecting relief, but simply to see if a professional could help him stop the endless, exhausting vigilance that had taken over his life.
